title: Classes, objects, enums, interfaces
scopeHtml: Scope: classes and objects, constructors and static members, enums with behaviour, interfaces as contracts, with before-and-after refactors.

notes.title: Classes and objects
notes.html:
A class is a blueprint; an object is one thing built from it. The class says "every Order has an id, a list of items and a status, and can add an item". Each new Order(...) makes a separate object with its own values. In an interview the real question is: what data belongs together, and which operations are allowed on it?

Mechanism (JVM): new Order() allocates memory on the heap (header ~12 to 16 bytes with compressed oops, then fields), runs the constructor, and gives you a reference (4 or 8 bytes) on the stack. Two variables can point at the same object, so a == b compares references, a.equals(b) compares meaning.

Before (a bag of data plus helpers everywhere):

class Order { public long id; public List<String> items = new ArrayList<>(); public String status; }

// somewhere else, in 6 different files:
order.items.add("shoes");
order.status = "PAID";            // typo "PADI" compiles fine
if (order.items.size() == 0) { /* forgot to block empty checkout */ }

After (the class guards its own rules):

final class Order {
    private final long id;
    private final List<String> items = new ArrayList<>();
    private Status status = Status.NEW;

    Order(long id) { this.id = id; }

    void addItem(String sku) {
        if (status != Status.NEW) throw new IllegalStateException("order is " + status);
        items.add(sku);
    }
    void pay() {
        if (items.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalStateException("empty order");
        status = Status.PAID;
    }
    enum Status { NEW, PAID, SHIPPED }
}
class Order(private val id: Long) {
    private val items = mutableListOf<String>()
    var status = Status.NEW
        private set
    fun addItem(sku: String) { check(status == Status.NEW) { "order is $status" }; items += sku }
    fun pay() { check(items.isNotEmpty()) { "empty order" }; status = Status.PAID }
    enum class Status { NEW, PAID, SHIPPED }
}

Worked example. An Order with 1 long, 1 list reference, 1 enum reference is about 32 bytes plus the ArrayList (about 40 bytes empty, 10-slot array on first add). A service holding 1M live orders in memory is roughly 100 to 150 MB for the shells alone, before item strings. That is why "just add another field" has a real cost at scale.

Industry examples. Stripe's PaymentIntent is an object with a strict state machine (requires_payment_method, succeeded...): you cannot jump states, the same idea as pay() above. Android's Activity is a class whose lifecycle methods are the only legal way to change its state.

Everyday analogy. A cookie cutter (class) and the cookies (objects). Each cookie can have different sprinkles, but the shape rules come from the cutter.

Decision gravity. Making fields private from day one is cheap and reversible. Exposing public fields is a one-way door: once 20 callers write order.status = ..., you cannot add validation without touching all of them.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing == and equals, and forgetting hashCode when overriding equals (breaks HashMap/HashSet).
  • Calling a class with only getters and setters "encapsulated"; it is a data bag with extra typing.
  • Saying objects live on the stack; references do, objects live on the heap (escape analysis may optimise this away, but never promise it).

notes.title: Constructors, static and instance members
notes.html:
Instance members belong to each object; static members belong to the class and exist once. A constructor makes sure an object is born valid: it is the only place you can guarantee every required field is set.

Mechanism: class loading runs static initialisers once, lazily on first use, thread-safely (the JVM holds a class-init lock). Instance initialisers and the constructor run on every new. Order: static init, then (per object) field initialisers, instance blocks, constructor body; a parent constructor always finishes before the child's.

// Before: half-built object, callers must remember to call setters
Email e = new Email();
e.setTo("a@b.com");   // forgot setSubject -> NullPointerException 3 calls later

// After: cannot exist invalid
record Email(String to, String subject) {
    Email { if (to == null || !to.contains("@")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad to"); }
}
data class Email(val to: String, val subject: String) {
    init { require("@" in to) { "bad to" } }
}

Worked example. Static mutable counter static int created used by 8 request threads: created++ is read, add, write, so 1,000,000 increments from 8 threads typically end near 600,000 to 900,000, not 1,000,000. Use AtomicInteger (CAS) or avoid static state.

Industry examples. Spring creates beans (singletons) via constructor injection so a bean is never half-wired. Google's Guava and Effective Java recommend static factory methods (List.of, Optional.of) when a name or caching helps.

Everyday analogy. A form that cannot be submitted until required boxes are filled, versus a form handed to you blank with "fill it in later, trust me".

Decision gravity. Constructors that enforce invariants are cheap now, painful to retrofit. Mutable static state is a trap you pay for in tests and concurrency; replace with injected dependencies (reversible, but touches many call sites).

Common interview traps.

  • Calling an overridable method from a constructor: the child's override runs before the child's fields are set and sees nulls or zeros.
  • Treating a static utility class as free: it cannot be mocked or swapped, so it hurts tests.
  • Forgetting that a static field is per classloader, not per JVM, in app servers.

notes.title: Enums that carry behaviour
notes.html:
An enum is a fixed set of named instances. Beginners use them as labels; seniors let each constant carry data and behaviour, which deletes whole switch ladders.

Mechanism: each constant is a singleton object created at class load. values() returns a fresh array copy each call. switch on an enum compiles to a lookup via ordinal(). EnumMap and EnumSet are array/bitset backed and much faster than HashMap/HashSet for enum keys.

Before (switch ladders copied in many places):

double fee(String type, double amount) {
    if (type.equals("CARD")) return amount * 0.02;
    else if (type.equals("UPI")) return 0;
    else if (type.equals("WALLET")) return amount * 0.01;
    throw new IllegalArgumentException(type);   // "Card" with a capital C also fails, at runtime
}

After (behaviour lives with the constant):

enum PaymentMethod {
    CARD   { double fee(double a) { return a * 0.02; } },
    UPI    { double fee(double a) { return 0; } },
    WALLET { double fee(double a) { return a * 0.01; } };
    abstract double fee(double amount);
}
double fee = PaymentMethod.valueOf("UPI").fee(500);   // 0.0
enum class PaymentMethod(private val rate: Double) {
    CARD(0.02), UPI(0.0), WALLET(0.01);
    fun fee(amount: Double) = amount * rate
}

Worked example. On Rs 1,000: CARD 20, UPI 0, WALLET 10. With a switch copied into billing, reporting and refunds, adding NETBANKING means 3 edits and 1 forgotten branch. With the enum it is 1 edit, and a switch expression without default makes the compiler flag a missing case.

Industry examples. java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit carries conversion logic per constant. HTTP status groups, Android Lifecycle.State and Stripe event types are all closed sets better modelled as enums or sealed types.

Everyday analogy. A vending machine's buttons: a fixed row of choices, each wired to its own action.

Decision gravity. Enum is right for a set that changes only with a code release. If ops must add values at runtime (a new country, a new payment partner from a config table), an enum is a one-way door; use a data row plus a strategy instead. Persist enums by name (EnumType.STRING), never ordinal: reordering constants silently corrupts stored data.

Common interview traps.

  • Storing ordinal() in the database.
  • Using enums for open-ended sets that grow weekly.
  • Not knowing enums can implement interfaces (but cannot extend classes) and are serialisation-safe singletons.

notes.title: Interfaces: the contract
notes.html:
An interface says WHAT can be done, not HOW. Callers depend on the contract, so the implementation can change without them noticing.

Mechanism: since Java 8 interfaces may have default and static methods, since Java 9 private methods. A class can implement many interfaces but extend one class. The JVM calls interface methods with invokeinterface, which is slightly slower than invokevirtual on a cold call but the JIT removes the difference when it sees one or two implementations at a call site.

Before (caller welded to one concrete class):

class CheckoutService {
    private final StripeClient stripe = new StripeClient("sk_live...");   // cannot test, cannot swap
    void pay(long cents) { stripe.charge(cents); }
}

After (depends on a contract; test uses a fake):

interface PaymentGateway { Receipt charge(long cents); }

class CheckoutService {
    private final PaymentGateway gateway;
    CheckoutService(PaymentGateway gateway) { this.gateway = gateway; }
    Receipt pay(long cents) { return gateway.charge(cents); }
}

class StripeGateway implements PaymentGateway { public Receipt charge(long c) { /* HTTP call */ return new Receipt(c); } }
class FakeGateway   implements PaymentGateway { public Receipt charge(long c) { return new Receipt(c); } }   // unit tests: 0 ms, no network
interface PaymentGateway { fun charge(cents: Long): Receipt }
class CheckoutService(private val gateway: PaymentGateway) { fun pay(cents: Long) = gateway.charge(cents) }
          +------------------+
          | CheckoutService  |
          +--------+---------+
                   | uses
                   v
          +------------------+
          | <<interface>>    |
          | PaymentGateway   |
          +--------+---------+
             ^             ^
             |             |
   +---------+--+    +-----+-------+
   | StripeGateway|  | FakeGateway |
   +-------------+   +-------------+

Worked example. Unit tests hitting a real sandbox payment API: about 400 ms each, flaky, 200 tests is 80 s. With the fake: about 1 ms each, 0.2 s total. Switching from Stripe to Razorpay changes one class and one wiring line.

Industry examples. JDBC (Connection, Statement) lets the same code talk to Postgres or MySQL. Android's Runnable, Comparable and Retrofit service interfaces are contracts whose implementation is generated or swapped.

Everyday analogy. A wall socket: any plug that fits works, and the house does not care which factory made the toaster.

Decision gravity. Do not create an interface for every class (FooImpl with one implementation and no test seam is noise). Create one where there is a real second implementation, a test seam or a module boundary. Adding an interface later is usually easy; removing a published public interface is a one-way door, since external code implements it. Adding an abstract method to a published interface breaks every implementer, which is why default methods exist.

Common interview traps.

  • Interface vs abstract class: interface for a capability/contract (no state), abstract class when subclasses share state and partial code.
  • Diamond problem with default methods: the class must override and can pick with A.super.hello().
  • Putting constants in an interface (the "constant interface" anti-pattern).

notes.title: Before and after: a full refactor
notes.html:
Put the pieces together on one small feature: "apply a discount to an order".

Before (everything in one place, string types, public data):

class OrderProcessor {
    double total(List<double[]> lines, String customerType) {
        double sum = 0;
        for (double[] l : lines) sum += l[0] * l[1];          // price * qty, what is l[2]?
        if (customerType.equals("VIP")) sum *= 0.9;
        else if (customerType.equals("EMP")) sum *= 0.8;
        return sum;
    }
}

Problems: magic arrays, strings that can typo, a new customer type edits this method (open to bugs), cannot test pricing without the processor.

After:

record Line(String sku, long unitCents, int qty) { long cents() { return unitCents * qty; } }

enum CustomerType {
    REGULAR(0), VIP(10), EMPLOYEE(20);
    private final int percentOff;
    CustomerType(int p) { percentOff = p; }
    long apply(long cents) { return cents - cents * percentOff / 100; }
}

final class PriceCalculator {
    long total(List<Line> lines, CustomerType type) {
        long sum = lines.stream().mapToLong(Line::cents).sum();
        return type.apply(sum);
    }
}
data class Line(val sku: String, val unitCents: Long, val qty: Int) { val cents get() = unitCents * qty }
enum class CustomerType(private val percentOff: Int) {
    REGULAR(0), VIP(10), EMPLOYEE(20);
    fun apply(cents: Long) = cents - cents * percentOff / 100
}
 Before:  OrderProcessor --> double[] , String
 After:   PriceCalculator --> Line (record) , CustomerType (enum)

Worked example. Lines: 2 x 49.99 and 1 x 20.00 is, in cents, 2 x 4999 + 2000 = 11998. VIP (10% off): 11998 * 10 / 100 = 1199 (integer division), so 11998 - 1199 = 10799 cents. Money in long cents avoids the 0.1 + 0.2 floating-point drift; never use double for money.

Industry examples. Shopify and Stripe both store money as integer minor units plus a currency code, for exactly this reason.

Everyday analogy. Cleaning a garage: labelled boxes (types) instead of one pile with a sticky note saying "stuff".

Decision gravity. Introducing value types (Line, CustomerType) is cheap, reversible and pays back immediately in readability and compile-time safety. Moving money from double to long after data exists in a database is a one-way migration, so choose before the first row.

Common interview traps.

  • Using double/float for currency.
  • Refactoring without a test first; write the characterisation test on the old code, then change.
  • Over-engineering: a PricingStrategyFactory for two discount types.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Class = blueprint, object = heap instance; == is reference identity, equals/hashCode define meaning.
  • Make fields private and let the class guard its own rules; public fields are a one-way door.
  • Constructors must produce valid objects; avoid mutable static state and calling overridable methods in constructors.
  • Enums can carry data and behaviour, replacing switch ladders; store by name, use EnumMap/EnumSet; avoid for runtime-growing sets.
  • Interfaces are contracts that enable swapping and testing; create them for real seams, not every class.
  • Refactor with value types, enums and integer money; write a test before changing behaviour.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between a class and an object, and between == and equals in Java?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you know references from objects, and whether you know why hashCode must follow equals.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A class is the blueprint, an object is one heap instance built from it. A variable holds a reference, so == asks "same object?" while equals asks "same meaning?". If I override equals I must override hashCode too, or HashMap and HashSet break.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
new Order(1) allocates on the heap (object header about 12 to 16 bytes, then fields), runs the constructor and returns a reference. Two variables can hold the same reference. == compares the references. Object.equals defaults to ==; value types such as Money override it to compare fields. HashMap picks a bucket from hashCode() first, then uses equals inside the bucket, so two equal objects with different hash codes land in different buckets and a lookup misses.

a ---> [Order id=1]      b ---> [Order id=1]   (a == b is false, a.equals(b) true if overridden)
c ---> same object as a  (a == c is true)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

record Money(long cents, String currency) { }          // equals/hashCode generated from fields
new Money(500, "INR").equals(new Money(500, "INR"));   // true
new Money(500, "INR") == new Money(500, "INR");        // false
data class Money(val cents: Long, val currency: String)
Money(500, "INR") == Money(500, "INR")    // true: Kotlin == calls equals
Money(500, "INR") === Money(500, "INR")   // false: === is reference identity

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Overriding equals without hashCode.
  • Saying objects live on the stack; the reference does, the object is on the heap.
  • Using a mutable field in hashCode and then mutating an object that is already in a HashSet.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does Kotlin == do? -> Calls equals; === is reference identity.
  2. Why does new String("a") == "a" print false? -> new forces a new object; the literal is the interned one.
  3. What is the contract between equals and hashCode? -> Equal objects must have equal hash codes; unequal objects may collide; both must be stable while the object is in a hash collection.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "== compares references". Senior adds the hash-bucket mechanism, records/data classes to generate both, and that mutable keys corrupt collections.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cache keyed by an entity with equals but no hashCode never hit; the team saw a 0% hit rate and doubled DB load.

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate's order code has been live for a month. Support reports orders stuck in status PADI and one empty order that was paid.

class Order { public long id; public List<String> items = new ArrayList<>(); public String status; }

// scattered over 6 files
order.items.add("shoes");
order.status = "PADI";
if (order.items.size() == 0) { /* forgot to block empty checkout */ }
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and how would you restructure the class?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add getters and setters." That keeps every rule outside the class and the typo still compiles inside setStatus(String).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which states are legal and in what order? Do other services read status? Is the table keyed by the string value?
  2. Immediate mitigation: One-off SQL to fix the PADI rows after confirming with support; add a DB CHECK constraint on status values.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Public mutable fields let any caller break rules (root cause); stringly-typed status; missing invariant "cannot pay an empty order".
  4. How I'd verify each: grep for \.status = and \.items\. across the repo; count writers; query SELECT status, count(*) GROUP BY status.
  5. Root cause: The class does not guard its own rules, so 6 files each re-implement them.
  6. Fix: Private fields, an enum Status, addItem and pay methods that validate.
final class Order {
    private final long id;
    private final List<String> items = new ArrayList<>();
    private Status status = Status.NEW;
    Order(long id) { this.id = id; }
    void addItem(String sku) { if (status != Status.NEW) throw new IllegalStateException("order is " + status); items.add(sku); }
    void pay() { if (items.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalStateException("empty order"); status = Status.PAID; }
    enum Status { NEW, PAID, SHIPPED }
}
class Order(private val id: Long) {
    private val items = mutableListOf<String>()
    var status = Status.NEW
        private set
    fun addItem(sku: String) { check(status == Status.NEW) { "order is $status" }; items += sku }
    fun pay() { check(items.isNotEmpty()) { "empty order" }; status = Status.PAID }
    enum class Status { NEW, PAID, SHIPPED }
}
  1. Prevention: Code review rule "no public mutable fields"; a unit test per illegal transition.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add a setter for status "for flexibility"; I would not rewrite all 6 files at once, I would migrate callers behind compile errors.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Another service needs to read status -> expose a getter returning the enum, not a setter.
  • Admin needs to force a state -> add an explicit adminCancel() method with an audit entry, not a raw setter.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A checkout bug let two code paths mark an order paid; refunds took a week to reconcile. Moving the rule into pay() made the second path throw in the first test run.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds getters/setters only.
  • Hire: private fields, enum, behaviour methods.
  • Strong hire: also DB constraint, migration plan, and one-way-door reasoning about public fields.

questions.promptHtml: In what order do static initialisers, field initialisers, instance blocks and constructors run, and why is calling an overridable method from a constructor dangerous?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It exposes whether you understand that a child's fields are not set while the parent constructor runs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Static init runs once at class load. Per new, the parent finishes first (fields, then constructor body), then the child's fields, then the child's constructor. If the parent constructor calls an overridable method, the child's override runs before the child's fields are set, so it sees nulls and zeros.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The JVM initialises a class lazily on first use under an init lock, so static init is thread-safe and runs once per classloader. Object creation zeroes all fields first, then runs the constructor chain from the top parent down. Virtual dispatch already uses the real runtime class, even in the parent constructor.

new Child():  Child static init (once) -> Parent fields -> Parent ctor -> Child fields -> Child ctor

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

class Parent { Parent() { init(); } void init() { } }
class Child extends Parent {
    private final List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
    @Override void init() { names.add("x"); }   // NullPointerException: names not yet assigned
}
open class Parent { init { init() } open fun init() {} }
class Child : Parent() {
    private val names = mutableListOf<String>()
    override fun init() { names += "x" }   // NullPointerException: names not yet assigned
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming the child's field initialisers ran before the parent constructor.
  • Putting I/O or thread starts in constructors (leaks this before it is built).
  • Forgetting statics are per classloader, not per JVM.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you fix it? -> Make the method final/private, or use a static factory that calls init() after construction.
  2. What does this escape mean? -> Passing this to another thread or listener from a constructor before it finishes.
  3. Is static init thread-safe? -> Yes, the class init lock guarantees one run; a cycle between two classes can still deadlock.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists the order. Senior shows the NPE, names this-escape, and prefers factories plus immutable fields.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A base class constructor called register() that a subclass overrode; the listener fired with half-built state and caused a NullPointerException only under Spring startup.

questions.contextHtml:
A service counts created orders for a dashboard. 8 request threads, 1,000,000 creations in a load test, the counter shows 712,340.

class OrderIdGenerator {
    static int created;
    static int next() { created++; return created; }
}

A second bug report: two orders got the same id in production.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make next synchronized and move on", without noting that static mutable state hurts tests and that ids should come from the DB or a unique source.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Single JVM or many? Must ids be dense or only unique? Is the counter reset on restart?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop using the counter as a primary key; rely on a DB sequence for uniqueness.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Non-atomic created++ (read, add, write) is the cause; visibility without volatile; multiple instances each starting at 0.
  4. How I'd verify each: Re-run the load test with AtomicInteger and compare; log (instance, id) pairs and look for duplicates across pods.
  5. Root cause: created++ is three steps; two threads read the same value and both write it, losing updates and issuing duplicate ids.
  6. Fix: Short-term AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet(). Long-term, avoid static state: inject an IdGenerator, back it with a DB sequence or a snowflake-style id for multi-instance.
class OrderIdGenerator {
    private final AtomicLong created = new AtomicLong();
    long next() { return created.incrementAndGet(); }
}
class OrderIdGenerator { private val created = AtomicLong(); fun next(): Long = created.incrementAndGet() }
  1. Prevention: A concurrent unit test (8 threads x 100k) asserting distinct ids; a review rule against mutable statics.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: synchronized also works but contends under load; I would not use a static counter across pods and call it unique.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• 40 pods now -> in-memory counters collide; use a DB sequence or ULID/snowflake.
  • Need the counter only for metrics -> LongAdder has lower contention than AtomicLong.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A promo-code generator used a static counter; after a deploy to 3 pods, 3 customers received identical single-use codes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cannot explain why the count is wrong.
  • Hire: names the race and uses AtomicInteger.
  • Strong hire: also covers multi-instance uniqueness and testability of static state.

questions.contextHtml:
After a release, 3,000 shipped orders show as NEW and 800 PAID orders show as SHIPPED. The change: a developer inserted REFUNDED in the middle of the enum.

enum Status { NEW, PAID, SHIPPED }          // before
enum Status { NEW, PAID, REFUNDED, SHIPPED } // after
@Enumerated(EnumType.ORDINAL) Status status;

The DB column is an int. No exception was thrown.
questions.promptHtml: What happened and how do you recover and prevent it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Roll back the deploy." That leaves the damage from rows already written under the new mapping.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: When was the deploy; how many rows were written since? Do we have a backup or event log? Which other tables store this enum?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the code to stop new wrong writes; freeze status-dependent jobs (shipping, refunds).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Ordinal shift (matches the symptoms exactly); a bad data migration; a cache serving old values.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare ordinal distribution before and after with SELECT status, count(*); diff the enum in git; check updated_at for rows changed after the deploy.
  5. Root cause: ORDINAL stores the position. Inserting a constant shifts every later value, so old 2 (SHIPPED) now reads as REFUNDED, old rows and new rows disagree.
  6. Fix: Restore from backup/audit log for rows written before the deploy window; switch to EnumType.STRING (or an explicit stable code). Add a migration that maps ints to names.
@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) private Status status;
@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) var status: Status = Status.NEW
  1. Prevention: Lint ban on EnumType.ORDINAL; a test that asserts stored names; append-only rule if a code must stay numeric.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just reorder constants back, because rows written under the new order are wrong in both mappings; I would not store names in a column too short for them.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Storage size matters (billions of rows) -> use an explicit code field, never the ordinal.
  • Renaming a constant -> with STRING storage, needs a migration; add the new name first, backfill, then remove.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A fraud rule enum stored by ordinal got a new constant at the top; for six hours "BLOCK" decisions were read as "REVIEW".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the deploy only.
  • Hire: identifies ordinal storage and switches to STRING.
  • Strong hire: data repair plan, lint rule and numeric-code alternative.

questions.contextHtml:
Billing, reporting and refunds each contain this ladder. Product now wants NETBANKING at 1.5% and UPI free up to Rs 2,000 then 0.5%.

double fee(String type, double amount) {
    if (type.equals("CARD")) return amount * 0.02;
    else if (type.equals("UPI")) return 0;
    else if (type.equals("WALLET")) return amount * 0.01;
    throw new IllegalArgumentException(type);
}
questions.promptHtml: Which classes change, and how would you design it so the next method costs one edit?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add two else if branches in the three places." Three edits, and one gets forgotten.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the fee threshold per transaction? Will ops add methods without a release? Currency and rounding rules?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; ship the change behind a test that pins current fees.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Fee rules belong with the payment method; the set of methods changes only with a release, so an enum fits.
  4. How I'd verify each: Characterisation tests: CARD on 1000 gives 20, UPI 0, WALLET 10.
  5. Root cause: Behaviour is separated from the type, so every new type touches every switch.
  6. Fix: Enum with behaviour, money as long cents.
enum PaymentMethod {
    CARD   { long fee(long c) { return c * 2 / 100; } },
    UPI    { long fee(long c) { return c <= 200_000 ? 0 : c * 5 / 1000; } },
    WALLET { long fee(long c) { return c / 100; } },
    NETBANKING { long fee(long c) { return c * 15 / 1000; } };
    abstract long fee(long cents);
}
enum class PaymentMethod {
    CARD { override fun fee(c: Long) = c * 2 / 100 },
    UPI { override fun fee(c: Long) = if (c <= 200_000) 0 else c * 5 / 1000 },
    WALLET { override fun fee(c: Long) = c / 100 },
    NETBANKING { override fun fee(c: Long) = c * 15 / 1000 };
    abstract fun fee(cents: Long): Long
}
  1. Prevention: switch expressions without default over this enum so the compiler flags missing cases elsewhere.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: If ops must add methods at runtime from config, an enum is a one-way door; I would use a table plus a strategy instead.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Fee varies by country -> add a second dimension; pass a FeePolicy, do not multiply enum constants.
  • Parse from API input -> valueOf throws on "Card"; validate and return 400.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A fourth wallet was added in billing but not in refunds; customers were refunded Rs 0 fee for two weeks until a switch missed a branch.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds branches in each place.
  • Hire: enum with abstract method.
  • Strong hire: also cents, compiler-checked switches, and the runtime-growth limit of enums.

questions.promptHtml: When do you choose an interface over an abstract class, and what happens when two default methods collide?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests judgement about contracts versus shared state, and knowledge of Java 8+ interface features.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An interface is a contract with no state that a class can combine many of; an abstract class is for subclasses that share state and partial code, and you get only one. If two interfaces give the same default method, the class must override it and can pick one with A.super.hello().

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Since Java 8 interfaces can have default and static methods, since 9 private ones, but still no instance fields. A class extends one class and implements many interfaces. Calls through an interface use invokeinterface; the JIT removes the cost when a call site sees one or two implementations. Default methods exist so you can add behaviour to a published interface without breaking implementers.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

interface A { default String hello() { return "A"; } }
interface B { default String hello() { return "B"; } }
class C implements A, B { public String hello() { return A.super.hello(); } }  // must resolve
interface A { fun hello() = "A" }
interface B { fun hello() = "B" }
class C : A, B { override fun hello() = super<A>.hello() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• FooImpl with one implementation and no test seam is noise, not design.
  • Constants in an interface (the constant-interface anti-pattern).
  • Using an abstract class when no state is shared, which blocks other inheritance.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can an interface have state? -> Only static final constants, no instance fields.
  2. Why did Java add default methods? -> To evolve interfaces such as Collection (stream()) without breaking implementers.
  3. Is removing a public interface easy? -> No, external code implements it; it is a one-way door.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "interface has no code". Senior frames it as state vs contract, mentions default-method conflicts, and API evolution.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A library added an abstract method to a public interface in a minor release and broke every downstream implementer at compile time.

questions.contextHtml:
200 unit tests for checkout call a real payment sandbox. Each takes about 400 ms, the suite takes 80 s, and fails roughly 1 run in 10 on network timeouts. The class:

class CheckoutService {
    private final StripeClient stripe = new StripeClient("sk_test_...");
    Receipt pay(long cents) { return stripe.charge(cents); }
}

Product also wants Razorpay support next quarter.
questions.promptHtml: How do you make this testable and swappable?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use Mockito's static mocking on StripeClient." That treats the symptom; the dependency is still hidden inside.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do we need a second gateway in production or only in tests? Where is the key loaded from? What is the failure contract (exceptions or result type)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Mark the sandbox tests as integration tests and run them nightly; stop blocking PRs on them.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Constructor-created dependency prevents substitution; secret in source; one test class does both unit and integration work.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the suite offline; it fails everywhere, proving the network dependence.
  5. Root cause: new StripeClient inside the class welds it to one concrete implementation.
  6. Fix: Extract an interface, inject it.
interface PaymentGateway { Receipt charge(long cents); }
class CheckoutService {
    private final PaymentGateway gateway;
    CheckoutService(PaymentGateway g) { this.gateway = g; }
    Receipt pay(long cents) { return gateway.charge(cents); }
}
class StripeGateway implements PaymentGateway { public Receipt charge(long c) { /* HTTP */ return new Receipt(c); } }
class FakeGateway implements PaymentGateway { public Receipt charge(long c) { return new Receipt(c); } }
interface PaymentGateway { fun charge(cents: Long): Receipt }
class CheckoutService(private val gateway: PaymentGateway) { fun pay(cents: Long) = gateway.charge(cents) }

Unit tests drop to about 1 ms each (0.2 s total). Keep 3 contract tests against the sandbox. 7. Prevention: Rule: no new of infrastructure clients inside services; a failing-gateway fake to test error paths. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add interfaces for every class, only at the real seam. I would not mock the HTTP library when my own interface is the better boundary.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Gateway sometimes times out -> add a FailingGateway fake and test the retry/idempotency policy.
  • Razorpay arrives -> one new class and one wiring line.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team whose CI took 25 minutes because of live API tests got it to 3 minutes after introducing one gateway interface.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: static mocking or skipping tests.
  • Hire: interface plus constructor injection with a fake.
  • Strong hire: also contract tests, failure fakes and restraint about over-abstracting.

questions.contextHtml:
A pricing module stores money as double in a DECIMAL-less FLOAT column and passes double[] lines around. A reconciliation job shows 1,300 orders a day differing by 1 paisa from the payment provider. 40 million rows exist; checkout runs 24x7 at 300 orders per minute.

0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004
sum 10 x 19.99 in double = 199.89999999999998
questions.promptHtml: How do you migrate to integer minor units with no downtime?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Round at the end." It hides drift and does not fix storage.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which currencies (0, 2 or 3 minor digits)? Which services read the column? Is there a replica or CDC consumer?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Compute totals in BigDecimal at the edges and round half-even once, so the daily drift stops while the migration runs.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Binary floating-point cannot represent 0.1; per-line rounding differs from the provider's; float column storage loses precision.
  4. How I'd verify each: Recompute a sample of 1,000 drifting orders with BigDecimal and compare against the provider file.
  5. Root cause: double for money; it is the same one-way door as any storage type.
  6. Fix: Expand/contract: add amount_minor BIGINT and currency columns; dual-write; backfill in batches of 10k with round(amount*100); verify counts and sums; switch reads; drop the old column later.
record Money(long minor, String currency) {
    Money plus(Money o) { if (!currency.equals(o.currency)) throw new IllegalArgumentException(); return new Money(minor + o.minor, currency); }
}
data class Money(val minor: Long, val currency: String) {
    operator fun plus(o: Money): Money { require(currency == o.currency); return Money(minor + o.minor, currency) }
}
  1. Prevention: A lint rule banning double in the pricing package; property tests on sums; daily reconciliation alert at > 0 mismatches.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not do a big-bang ALTER TYPE on 40M rows in a locking migration; I would not switch reads before verifying both columns agree.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Currency with 3 decimals (KWD) -> store the scale per currency.
  • Percentage discounts -> define the rounding rule (half-even) and where it applies, per line or total.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team found Rs 14 lakh a year of rounding drift only after a finance audit; the fix took 3 weeks because no one owned the column type.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "just round".
  • Hire: long cents or BigDecimal with a staged migration.
  • Strong hire: dual-write/backfill/verify, per-currency scale, and a prevention rule.

questions.promptHtml: When is an enum the right model and when is it a trap? What do EnumMap and EnumSet give you?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests the open/closed boundary: release-time sets versus runtime-growing sets.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An enum fits a closed set that changes only with a code release, and it can carry data and behaviour. If ops must add values at runtime, such as a new payment partner from a config table, an enum is a one-way door and I would use a row plus a strategy. EnumMap and EnumSet are array and bitset backed, faster than hash collections.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each constant is a singleton created at class load; values() returns a copy every call, so cache it in hot code. switch on an enum maps through the ordinal. Enums can implement interfaces but not extend classes. Persist by name, never ordinal. A switch expression without default makes the compiler flag new constants.

Need Choice
Fixed set, changes with release enum with behaviour
Set grows from config/DB table row + Strategy keyed by id
Sum type with different data per case sealed interface + records

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

EnumMap<PaymentMethod, Long> fees = new EnumMap<>(PaymentMethod.class);
EnumSet<PaymentMethod> instant = EnumSet.of(PaymentMethod.UPI, PaymentMethod.WALLET);
val fees = EnumMap<PaymentMethod, Long>(PaymentMethod::class.java)
val instant = EnumSet.of(PaymentMethod.UPI, PaymentMethod.WALLET)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling values() in a hot loop (new array each call).
  • Using an enum for a set that gains values weekly.
  • Trying to make an enum extend a class.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is EnumMap faster? -> It is an array indexed by ordinal, no hashing.
  2. How do you add a constant safely? -> Append, persist by name, update exhaustive switches.
  3. Enum vs sealed types? -> Sealed lets each case carry different fields and be created many times; enum constants are singletons.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE uses enums as labels. Senior puts behaviour on them, names the runtime-growth limit and the storage rule.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A country enum needed a hotfix deploy every time sales opened a market; moving it to a table ended the release dependency.

questions.contextHtml: You own an internal SDK interface Notifier { void send(String userId, String text); } implemented by 14 teams' services. You need sendBatch(List<String> ids, String text) and want a Priority argument eventually.
questions.promptHtml: How do you add this without breaking 14 teams, and what do you avoid?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add the abstract methods and tell teams to update." That is a compile break across 14 repos on release day.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Source or binary compatibility needed? Are there external implementers? Who owns deprecation?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; plan a compatible release.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Default method gives a working fallback; a new sub-interface for the new capability; an options object to avoid signature churn.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compile 3 sample implementers against the new SDK, and run a binary-compat check tool in CI (verify tool choice).
  5. Root cause: Adding an abstract method changes the contract for every implementer.
  6. Fix: A default method delegating to the old one; take an options object for future args.
interface Notifier {
    void send(String userId, String text);
    default void sendBatch(List<String> ids, String text) { ids.forEach(id -> send(id, text)); }
}
interface Notifier {
    fun send(userId: String, text: String)
    fun sendBatch(ids: List<String>, text: String) = ids.forEach { send(it, text) }
}

Teams that can do better batching override it. 7. Prevention: API review checklist; semantic versioning; deprecate with a date; contract tests. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add an abstract method; I would not publish a Priority enum parameter on every overload now (YAGNI) but would reserve an options object if a second parameter is already known.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A team already has a sendBatch with a different meaning -> compile fails or semantics clash; check usage first, version the SDK.
  • Two interfaces both provide the default -> implementer must resolve with X.super.m().

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An abstract method added in a patch release broke 9 services in one night; the rollback was a revert plus a postmortem on API reviews.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds the abstract method.
  • Hire: default method.
  • Strong hire: also compatibility checks, deprecation process and options-object reasoning.

questions.contextHtml:
A PR "refactors" pricing. Old code:

double total(List<double[]> lines, String customerType) {
    double sum = 0;
    for (double[] l : lines) sum += l[0] * l[1];
    if (customerType.equals("VIP")) sum *= 0.9;
    else if (customerType.equals("EMP")) sum *= 0.8;
    return sum;
}

The PR adds PricingStrategyFactory, AbstractDiscountProvider and a plugin registry, and changes double to long cents in one commit with no new tests. Lines 2 x 4999 and 1 x 2000 should give VIP 10799.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "LGTM, looks cleaner." It misses missing tests and speculative layers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are more than two discount types actually planned? Where is rounding defined? Are stored values already in double?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Block merging until a characterisation test pins current outputs.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Behaviour change hidden in the type change (rounding); speculative generality; stringly typed input remains.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run old and new on 10,000 random carts and diff; compute VIP: 11998 - 11998*10/100 (integer division 1199) = 10799.
  5. Root cause: Several refactors in one commit with no safety net.
  6. Fix: Split: (a) characterisation tests, (b) value types Line and CustomerType enum, (c) cents migration with a stated rounding rule.
record Line(String sku, long unitCents, int qty) { long cents() { return unitCents * qty; } }
enum CustomerType {
    REGULAR(0), VIP(10), EMPLOYEE(20);
    private final int off; CustomerType(int o) { off = o; }
    long apply(long cents) { return cents - cents * off / 100; }
}
final class PriceCalculator { long total(List<Line> l, CustomerType t) { return t.apply(l.stream().mapToLong(Line::cents).sum()); } }
data class Line(val sku: String, val unitCents: Long, val qty: Int) { val cents get() = unitCents * qty }
enum class CustomerType(private val off: Int) {
    REGULAR(0), VIP(10), EMPLOYEE(20);
    fun apply(cents: Long) = cents - cents * off / 100
}
  1. Prevention: PR template: "tests first for refactors"; limit PR size.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not keep the factory and registry for two discount types; extract an interface when the third real rule appears.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Rounding of 10% on odd cents -> state half-even or floor explicitly and test it.
  • A new "STUDENT" type -> one enum constant and one test.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "cleanup" PR changed rounding from per-line to per-order; revenue shifted by 0.02% and finance spent a week finding it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: approves.
  • Hire: asks for tests and removes speculative layers.
  • Strong hire: also splits the change, verifies numerically and names rounding policy.
